title: Example report: two synthetic communities
text:
Question and inputs
How do community composition and diversity differ between two groups? This synthetic dataset contains 24 samples, 12 per group, and 15 fictional features. Feature-table totals range from 3299 to 11964. These totals are not verified raw sequencing depth.
crumbs: 2  Example report: two synthetic communities

title: Example report: two synthetic communities
text:
Methods
Validate identifiers and counts, calculate sample feature proportions, observed richness, and Shannon diversity using natural logarithms. The composition display retains the top eight features by mean sample proportion; all others become Other. Diversity uses all 15 features. No inferential tests are performed.

title: Example report: two synthetic communities
text:
Limits and conclusion






Note



These are synthetic data. Higher diversity does not imply better health, and visual group differences do not establish significance or causation. Real studies require review of sampling effort, filtering, contamination, study design, and suitable statistical methods.

title: Verify and explain
text:
Check one sample yourself
From the repository root, run this command in your terminal at the shell prompt:
Rscript scripts/R/05-verify-sample.R
The script checks A01 by default. Open scripts/R/05-verify-sample.R in your editor to follow the calculation.

Add the counts for A01 and count how many features have a positive count.
Divide each feature count by the sample total to get its proportion.
Use the positive proportions to calculate Shannon diversity with natural logarithms.
Compare all three results with the saved row for A01.

title: Verify and explain
text:
Expected output
All three rows should show TRUE in agrees. For the supplied example, Shannon diversity rounds to 2.423797. Compare the unrounded values in code; small rounding differences in displayed tables are normal.
If a check fails, confirm that you used the same input folder, output folder, and sample ID as the analysis. Rerun the analysis after changing an input table.

From output to evidence
You have reproduced one sample’s summaries from its counts and compared them with the saved results. You can now explain how those numbers were obtained.

text:
Repeat with your own data
Use a separate folder for your input tables and a separate output folder. Run the analysis first, then use those same folders and a sample ID from your count table when you run the verification script.

title: Verify and explain
text:
Explain the figures
These figures are generated by the data/my-study/ analysis above.



Relative taxonomic composition of the study samples.


Compare the proportions of the same taxa across samples. The “Other” category pools taxa for display, so use the underlying table to see which taxa contribute to it.



Feature count totals and diversity for the study samples.


Check whether samples with higher count totals also tend to have higher diversity. Sample-214 had more counts than Sample-32 (19,040 vs. 10,585) but lower Shannon diversity. Use the full plot to judge whether there is an overall pattern.



Shannon diversity across the study groups.


Compare the spread and overlap of the values across groups. Sample-32 and Sample-214 both had 103 observed features, but Sample-32 had higher Shannon diversity (3.17 vs. 2.03), reflecting greater evenness in its feature counts. This comparison describes two samples.

What varies within and between groups?
Do diversity values overlap?
Could count totals, filtering, or study design affect interpretation?
Which claims cannot be supported?

title: Verify and explain
section: Use AI to review your interpretation
text:
Use AI to review your interpretation
Inspect the figures and tables first. Then supply the relevant outputs to your AI assistant with this prompt:

I am comparing community composition and diversity between two groups using 24 synthetic samples and 15 fictional features. Using only the figures and tables I supply, help me describe the patterns in composition, diversity, and count totals. Check whether your descriptions agree with the numerical values. Identify limitations and questions I should investigate. Do not invent results or claim statistical significance or causation from visual differences alone.

For your own study, replace the sample and feature details with your actual study information.
Compare the response with the outputs. Check group labels, numerical values, and figure axes. Count totals describe the supplied counts; they do not by themselves measure absolute microbial abundance.
In results/decision-log.md, record briefly:

AI suggested: the explanation or change proposed.
I verified: the output, calculation, or code you checked.
I decided: what you accepted, revised, or rejected, and why.

For your own study, save this record beside its outputs, for example in results/my-study/decision-log.md.






Note



Higher diversity does not automatically mean a healthier community. Visual differences do not establish significance or causation.

title: Appendix B — Community comparison: get ready
text:
Prepare your environment
Question: How do community composition and diversity vary between two groups?
Inputs: 24 synthetic samples, 12 per group, and 15 fictional features.
Finish with: composition, diversity, and count-total figures; checked tables; a short report.
This is a descriptive teaching example. Visual differences alone do not establish statistical significance or causation. When adapting it, check that the methods suit your study design.
To explore without installing software, open See the result. To reproduce the analysis, complete the setup below once.
You need R, Quarto, and a text editor such as VS Code or RStudio.

title: Appendix B — Community comparison: get ready
text:
Open the project root
Download and extract the repository, then open the folder containing _quarto.yml, renv.lock, data/, and scripts/ in your editor.
Open a terminal in that folder. Run every command in this example from this project root, including commands shown on pages stored inside examples/.


Restore the R environment
In the terminal, start R:
R
At the R prompt (>), run:
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("renv")
}

renv::restore()
renv::status()
If asked to proceed, enter Y and wait for the > prompt before entering another command. Restore the supplied lockfile rather than initializing a new environment.
Check that the analysis packages load, then return to the terminal:
library(tidyverse)
library(vegan)

q(save = "no")






Note



If setup fails: copy the error message. Ask AI to explain it using your R version, operating system, and the command you ran. Check the proposed fix before applying it. Keep the supplied lockfile intact while investigating.

title: Appendix C — Technical appendix
text:
Requirements
R, Quarto, and the packages recorded in root renv.lock. Restore with renv::restore(). The domain uses one shared environment.

title: Appendix C — Technical appendix
text:
Reuse
Both scripts accept optional input and output directories. Run from the repository root. Keep original study data separate from data/example/.
Feature tables must contain integer counts. Metadata must include sample_id and group; taxonomy must include matching feature_id and nonblank taxon. Zero-total samples fail validation.

title: Appendix C — Technical appendix
text:
Scope
The workflow starts from a feature table. It does not process raw reads, assign taxonomy, test group significance, adjust for repeated measures or confounding, or perform differential abundance analysis.
Included preview figures and tables were computed independently with Python. Run the supplied R scripts to regenerate equivalent numerical summaries and R-styled figures. Quarto code fences do not execute analysis.
